proposals.name: Pun anchored in a documented fact about the named subject
proposals.instruction: Score how far the entry's second meaning is licensed by something specifically true of the real person, institution or event it names, rather than by sound alone. 10 = the double-meaning word is simultaneously (a) idiomatic in the sentence and (b) a precise, checkable comment on that subject's known conduct, role or predicament, so the reader must retrieve a real fact to complete the joke. 5 = a named subject appears but the wordplay would work about equally well with a different name substituted. 0 = no named subject, or the name is decorative and the pun rests only on letter or sound similarity. Judge only the text; do not reward whether the reference is one you personally recognize, only whether the entry commits to a specific, factual hook.
proposals.rationale: The densest cluster of dense-high/card-low rows is exactly this shape: R08 ('disappointedly' encodes dis-appointed, which is literally Zoe Baird's situation), R39 ('circumspectly' about John Bobbitt), R41 ('cordially' about Ted Kennedy), R46 ('absently' about a coach missing the playoffs), R57 ('plainly' about Janet Reno's appearance). A scorecard that scores 'contains wordplay' and 'references a famous person' as separate boxes gets these right for the wrong reason and cannot distinguish them from R09 ('Peace Corpse') or R51 ('Profiles in Scourge'), where the famous referent contributes nothing beyond spelling.

proposals.name: Misdirection with a clean late flip
proposals.instruction: Score how strongly the entry first invites one confident reading and then, at a specific late word or phrase, forces a different reading that retroactively makes the whole text true. 10 = the reader is decisively led down one path, the pivot is a single identifiable moment, and after the flip every earlier element is re-explained rather than discarded. 5 = there is a twist but it is signposted early or the earlier text does not need re-reading. 0 = single-pass reading with no re-interpretation available. Do not reward mere obscurity or a text that is confusing on both readings.
proposals.rationale: R05 reads as a Fugitive plot summary until the attribution reveals Peter Pan and Captain Hook, at which point the whole sentence becomes literally true; R24 ('Adam and Eve: It Had to Be You') reads as a stock love-song title until the reader realizes there was no alternative partner in existence. Both are dense-high/card-low. Nothing in the card-high half has this structure: R25, R33, R38 all deliver their entire content on first read.

proposals.name: Self-demonstrating execution (the entry enacts its own claim)
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry performs the property it is talking about, so that its form and its content collide. 10 = the text is an instance of the very thing it names or denies, and the collision is the joke (e.g. a word that violates its own definition, a statement whose confident structure is exactly what makes its content vacuous). 5 = form and content are consistent but the form adds a small extra layer. 0 = form is a neutral container for the content. Score the collision, not general cleverness.
proposals.rationale: R34 ('Monosyllabic' as an oxymoron) is a five-syllable word meaning one-syllable; R26 and R44 are Yogi-isms whose grammar is impeccably assertive while the proposition is either a tautology or self-cancelling. All three are dense-high/card-low. A criterion bank built around topic, cleverness and clarity will not see that the sentence is doing something to itself; it will just see a short quoted sentence.

proposals.name: Complete joke payload versus setup-only stem
proposals.instruction: Score whether the text in front of you actually contains a comic payload or only the frame that would precede one. 10 = the entry is self-sufficient: a reader with no further material has everything needed for the joke to land. 5 = the payload is present but leans on an unstated shared referent that a general reader might not supply. 0 = the text is only a heading, category label, colon-terminated introduction, or announcement of a joke that never arrives. Judge presence of payload, not length.
proposals.rationale: A large share of the card-high/dense-low half is pure frame: R17 ('In a letter I received from Russia after visiting my pen pals:'), R20 ('Something That Will Never Become'), R35 ('A Political Slogan That Will Never Make It:'), R40 ('Something That Will Never Become an Olympic Sport --'). These read as on-brief, grammatical and topic-appropriate, which is exactly what a well-formedness-oriented card rewards, but they contain no joke at all. Contrast R13 and R22, which are complete.

proposals.name: Novelty versus stock gag already in circulation
proposals.instruction: Score how likely it is that this exact joke, or a near-identical version, already existed before the entry was written. 10 = the construction appears newly minted for this prompt; you cannot recall or easily reconstruct a prior version. 5 = a familiar template filled with a somewhat fresh instance. 0 = a proverb, bumper-sticker line, standard groaner or long-circulating pun reproduced essentially unchanged. Penalize the stock item even when it is well-formed and perfectly on-brief; reward novelty even when the execution is rough.
proposals.rationale: R52 ('Being nice isn't easy, and being easy isn't nice') is a textbook-perfect chiasmus and sits at card_pct 0.959, but it is a saying that predates the contest; R04 ('WordPrefect') and R58 ('Larry of Arabia') are the first pun anyone reaches for on those targets, at card 0.884 and 0.965. A card scoring symmetry, cleanness and fit will max these out; a reader who has seen them before will not. R09 and R25 are the same pattern.

proposals.name: Pun depth: both senses alive versus surface letter distortion
proposals.instruction: Score the mechanism of any wordplay. 10 = both senses of the pivot word or phrase are fully grammatical and fully meaningful in context at the same time, with no distortion of spelling or sound required. 5 = a homophone substitution where the new sense is meaningful but the original phrase has been altered. 0 = a single letter, syllable or vowel has been changed to make a nonsense or merely rude variant of a known name, and the resulting phrase means nothing coherent on its own. A judge should ask: if I hid the source phrase, would the result still parse as language?
proposals.rationale: The card-high half is dominated by single-character distortions: R38 ('The Heimlich Manure'), R09 ('Peace Corpse'), R51 ('Profiles in Scourge'), R16 ('Buttdragging Grasshound'). The dense-high half uses undistorted double-duty words: R47 ('categorically' about a Jeopardy host), R21 ('aimlessly' about a wild pitcher), R43 ('Low-Speed Chase'). Both look like 'wordplay' to a bank that counts wordplay rather than grading it.

proposals.name: Found phrase reframed rather than invented
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry takes an existing, unaltered phrase from the world and makes it funny purely by placing it in the contest's frame. 10 = the phrase is quoted exactly as it exists in ordinary use, and the entire comic work is done by the new frame, which reveals a property the phrase always had but nobody had named. 5 = an existing phrase is used but with modification or added scaffolding. 0 = the entry manufactures a novel string that has no life outside this entry. Note that this criterion can be high while surface effort looks near zero.
proposals.rationale: Several dense-high/card-low rows are unmodified found phrases whose only intervention is the frame: R03 ('Yom Kippur' offered as an oxymoron), R06 ('I'M WITH STUPID' on a self-mocking contest T-shirt), R30 ('U.N. Resolution'), R43 ('Low-Speed Chase'), R55 ('Chuck 3:16'). To a scorecard these look like the lowest-effort submissions in the pool - no construction, no elaboration - which plausibly drives their low card percentiles despite dense percentiles of 0.79 to 0.95.

proposals.name: Comic economy: payoff per word
proposals.instruction: Score the ratio of comic yield to text length. 10 = every word is load-bearing and the entry could not be shortened without destroying the joke; typically very short. 5 = some setup is doing necessary work but a few phrases could be cut. 0 = the entry explains, elaborates, or narrates at length around a joke that could have been delivered in a fraction of the words, or pads to reach a form. Length alone is not the score: a long entry whose length is the joke scores high, a short entry with a dead word scores low.
proposals.rationale: R24 delivers a complete premise in six words and R34 in one; both are dense-high/card-low. The card-high side contains the two longest, most explanatory items in the slice: R32 (a three-clause anecdote that walks the reader through its own reasoning) and R60 (a heavily front-loaded question whose punchline is a name). A rubric with per-criterion elaboration or completeness scoring systematically rewards the ones that talk more.

proposals.name: Contest constraint made load-bearing
proposals.instruction: Score whether the specific formal constraint the prompt imposes is doing comic work, as opposed to merely being satisfied or quietly dropped. 10 = the required form is the reason the joke works; remove the constraint and the joke evaporates. 5 = the form is satisfied correctly but the joke would survive translation into any other form. 0 = the form is violated outright (the required shape is absent), or is satisfied only as boilerplate. Judge the interaction of form and joke, not compliance by itself.
proposals.rationale: R47 needs the Tom Swiftly adverb slot for 'categorically' to detonate, and R05 needs the prompt's 'literally true and defensible' requirement for the Peter Pan reading to be the point; both are dense-high. On the other side, the Jeopardy prompt demands a question and R07, R53 and R02 supply bare answers, while R10 and R19 supply grammatically correct questions in which the interrogative form contributes nothing. A compliance-checking card scores form presence, so it cannot separate load-bearing form from inert form, and it may not even penalize the outright violations if it checks topic rather than shape.

proposals.name: Specific topical or local reference used accurately
proposals.instruction: Score the specificity and apparent accuracy of any real-world reference. 10 = names a particular person, case, team, agency or local place, and the detail invoked is precise enough that getting it wrong would break the joke. 5 = a broad category reference (politicians, lawyers, a sport) with no particular instance. 0 = no real-world anchor, or a reference so vague it could be swapped for any other. Reward precision of anchoring; do not reward or penalize how obscure the reference is.
proposals.rationale: R23 pairs two specific accused spies with a song title that only works given that fact; R59 names a specific fertility doctor whose scandal supplies the entire endorsement joke; R43 depends on one particular televised pursuit. All dense-high/card-low. The card-high half is anchored much more loosely - R14 ('Some Kittens Can Fly!'), R12 ('Lesser Hyattsville'), R29 ('USS Powderkeg') - yet reads as clean and confident, which is what a topicality-as-checkbox criterion measures.

proposals.name: Edge with a target versus shock as the whole joke
proposals.instruction: This is a composite. Score jointly (a) whether the entry takes a real risk - darkness, cruelty, taboo, or a swipe at a specific party - and (b) whether that risk is aimed at something, i.e. the transgressive element carries a point rather than being the punchline itself. 10 = genuinely edgy and the edge is pointed at a deserving or at least identifiable target, so the discomfort is doing comic work. 5 = safe and pleasant, no risk taken. 0 = transgressive material with no target, where the rude or leering element is the entire content and would collapse if the shock were removed. Note the scale is not monotone in edginess: score the pairing.
proposals.rationale: R13 kills its subject via a denied insurance claim, R39 and R57 aim genuine cruelty at specific named figures, R59 jokes about a fertility fraud; all are dense-high/card-low, and all point their edge somewhere. R56 is the counter-case on the card-high side (card 0.985): it is by far the most transgressive item in the slice but the leer is the whole joke. A one-directional 'boldness' or 'daring' criterion would rank R56 at the top, which is precisely the over-credit direction we see.

proposals.name: Airtight premise the reader cannot argue with
proposals.instruction: Score how completely the entry closes off objection once its premise is seen. 10 = the claim is undeniably and exactly true under the reading the entry intends; a skeptical reader who tries to poke at it finds the entry has already accounted for the objection. 5 = the premise mostly holds but requires the reader to grant one convenient assumption. 0 = the premise is loose, approximate, or only sort-of fits, so the reader must supply charity for it to work. Judge tightness of fit between the claim and reality, not how funny it is.
proposals.rationale: R24 is unanswerable (there was literally no one else it could have been), R05 satisfies its prompt's demand for literal defensibility on a strict reading, and R34 is true by inspection of the word itself. All dense-high/card-low. The card-high items are looser by construction: R28 ('Precision Pi Calculator') and R33 ('Java Screen Freezer') are plausible-sounding bad names but nothing about them is exactly right, and a card grading 'fits the category' registers no difference between exact and approximate fit.

proposals.name: Delivers without explaining or winking at itself
proposals.instruction: Score whether the entry trusts the reader. 10 = the joke is delivered and stops; no gloss, no signalled cleverness, no commentary on its own construction or on the contest. 5 = a small amount of scaffolding or an unnecessary tag. 0 = the entry narrates the mechanism of its own joke, hedges it, or spends its text on meta-commentary about entering the contest instead of on the bit. A raised eyebrow at the reader counts against; confident deadpan counts for.
proposals.rationale: R32 spends most of its length explaining the emotional logic of its own punchline and doing so about the contest itself, and R11 likewise trades on contest-meta rather than on the valentine; both sit above card 0.83 while dense places them near 0.33 and 0.42. The deadpan dense-high items - R26, R44, R24 - say the thing once and stop. Length-and-development-sensitive rubrics reward the self-narrating entries because there is visibly more reasoning on the page.

proposals.name: Prosodic craft sustained through a terminal payoff
proposals.instruction: This is a composite. Score jointly (a) whether meter, rhyme, or parallel structure is actually executed rather than merely attempted, and (b) whether the strongest comic beat falls at the final position. 10 = the form scans and rhymes cleanly (including a strained rhyme whose strain is itself enjoyable) and the last word or phrase is the payoff. 5 = competent form with the payoff buried mid-text, or a good final beat inside sloppy form. 0 = form collapses, or the entry trails off before any final beat. Score the joint condition, not either half alone.
proposals.rationale: R13 sustains limerick meter through a deliberately tortured rhyme and lands its darkest beat on the final word, and R22 escalates a list to a single closing pun that reinterprets the whole poem; both dense-high/card-low. Card-high verse entries are structurally flatter: R11 has no terminal payoff of its own and R45 is a title with no body. Separate 'form' and 'humor' criteria will each give partial credit to the flat cases, and neither will notice that the good cases are timing the payoff.

proposals.name: Wit present independent of surface polish
proposals.instruction: Score whether, after setting aside grammaticality, clean phrasing, correct topic, plausible tone and the presence of an attribution, any identifiable comic mechanism remains. 10 = a mechanism is clearly identifiable and could be named in a sentence (a reversal, a double meaning, an absurd literalization, a self-contradiction). 5 = a faint or conventional mechanism. 0 = the entry is polished, on-brief and entirely inert - nothing about it is trying to be funny beyond fitting the category. Explicitly do not credit tidiness, professional register, or looking like a real published example.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('Detroit Embarrassed by Pacers') is a clean, publishable-looking sports headline with card 0.967 and dense 0.431 - it satisfies the brief perfectly and contains no joke. R28 and R29 have the same profile: well-formed, plausible, comically empty. This is the clearest signature of scorecard over-credit in the slice, and it suggests the bank is rewarding surface competence that a reader treats as a floor rather than as evidence of quality.

proposals.name: Extent of attached author-credit apparatus
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH author-credit apparatus is physically present in the item text, counting only what you can see. 10 = a full parenthetical credit with personal name and locality attached to the entry (e.g. a trailing '(First Last, Town)'). 5 = a partial or truncated credit, a name without locality, or a locality without a name. 0 = no credit apparatus of any kind; the text is the entry alone. Count characters on the page, nothing else. You must NOT judge whether having a credit is good, whether the entry deserves one, or anything about the named person; do not let the presence or absence of a credit influence any impression of the entry's merit. This is a pure extent count of an apparatus feature.
proposals.rationale: Credit presence is unevenly distributed across the two disagreement halves in a way that has nothing to do with the joke: R51 ('Detroit Embarrassed by Pacers (Sandra Hull, Arlington)') and R12 ('Golden Reliever (Dudley Thompson, Silver Spring)') are card-high and fully credited, while R17 (the Tysons Corner limerick, dense 0.981) and R11 ('(Cartoon E) --', dense 0.998) carry no credit at all. Whether the record was captured with its byline is a property of the scrape and the page layout, not of the entry as an entry. A text-only model can read the byline and any correlated grouping straight off the surface, so it must be declared and discounted.
proposals.upstream_parent: source-record capture and typesetting provenance (whether the item was scraped from a context that carried its printed credit line)

proposals.name: Joint-byline and recurring-name fingerprint in the credit
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW STRONGLY the visible credit apparatus signals a practised or collaborating submitter rather than a one-off individual. 10 = two or more named submitters sharing one entry, a household pair, or a semicolon-joined multi-person credit. 5 = a single named submitter whose name or locality is formatted with unusual completeness (middle initial, out-of-state qualifier, formal styling). 0 = a plain single name, or no credit at all. Score only what the credit string looks like. You must NOT judge whether collaboration or practice is good, must not speculate about the person's skill, and must not let this affect any read on the entry's humour.
proposals.rationale: The slice contains several joint credits - R29 ('Sandra Hull, Arlington, and Stu Solomon, Springfield'), R44 ('Paul Styrene, Olney; Elden Carnahan, Laurel'), R42 ('Michelle and Warren Uhler'), R52 ('Andrea and Alan Pendleton') - and visible name recurrence across items, with 'Paul Kondis, Alexandria' credited on both R40 and R41 and a Sorensen of Herndon on both R20 and R35. A practised entrant is plausibly upstream of both the credit-string shape and, honestly, of writing better entries, so this is tagged mixed; but the fingerprint itself is a byline formatting feature and must never be creditable in the bank.
proposals.upstream_parent: the submitter's practice and social organisation in this format (habitual entrants, entrant pairs, entrant circles)

proposals.name: In-group reference to the column and its rituals
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text refers to the contest itself, its running jokes, its recurring apparatus, or the experience of entering it, as opposed to referring only to the world outside. 10 = the column, its prizes, its rituals, its regulars or its self-mocking house identity are the explicit subject of the text. 5 = a passing venue-insider allusion or a coinage that only parses to someone who reads the column regularly. 0 = no reference to the contest or its community anywhere in the text. Score presence and prominence of the in-group reference only. You must NOT judge whether the self-reference is charming, tiresome, or well-executed, and must not treat insider fluency as evidence of quality.
proposals.rationale: In-group reference lands on both sides of the disagreement and so is predictive without being about the entry's merit: R54 ('Entering the Style Invitational: I used to enter Publishers Clearing House sweepstakes...') and R53 ('I love you more than The Style Invitational') are card-high, while R43 ('Chuck 3:16') and R55 ('I'M WITH STUPID', both from the contest's own T-shirt prompt) are dense-high, and R08 ('Pub-it: n. A unit of measure...') coins a house term. The upstream factor - community tenure - plausibly also improves real entries, hence mixed=true.
proposals.upstream_parent: the submitter's embeddedness in the column's readership community (how long and how closely they have followed it)

proposals.name: Segmentation artifact: truncation and container-label prefixes
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text shows signs of having been cut out of a larger record rather than standing as a whole submission. 10 = the text is unmistakably a fragment: it breaks off mid-sentence or mid-phrase, ends in a bare dash or colon with nothing after it, or consists only of an item label carried over from the surrounding layout (e.g. a parenthetical figure label or a numbered quote header) with no body. 5 = the text is grammatically complete but opens with a carried-over label, prefix or numbering that is clearly part of the container's layout rather than of the entry. 0 = a clean, self-contained string with no layout residue and no truncation. Score the mechanical evidence of cutting only. You must NOT judge whether a fragment is a bad entry, and must not infer merit or its absence from the fragment's content.
proposals.rationale: Fragments occupy the extreme tail of the dense percentiles in this slice - R09 ('(Cartoon A) This is a beguiling', 0.999), R11 ('(Cartoon E) --', 0.998), R39 ('(Cartoon D) --', 0.997), R50 ('Quote 1: You will rejoice to hear...', 0.975) - while a different family of fragments sits at the top of the card percentiles, e.g. R46 ('Something That Will Never Become an Olympic Sport --') and R15 ('A Political Slogan That Will Never Make It:'). Both extremes are being driven by how the row was cut, not by any property of an entry, which makes this the clearest declared nuisance in the slice.
proposals.upstream_parent: record segmentation - how the printed column was split into individual item rows during corpus construction

proposals.name: Identifiability of the recurring contest-format template
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW STRONGLY the text conforms to a single, immediately recognisable recurring submission template, such that a reader could name the format from the shape of the string alone. 10 = the item is a textbook instance of one rigid recurring template (for example a quoted line of dialogue followed by 'said <Famous Name> <adverb>'; a short interrogative ending in a question mark; a two-word capitalised coinage). 5 = the item belongs to a loose genre with no fixed surface shape. 0 = free-form text with no template signature. Score template conformity, i.e. how mechanically the surface shape is determined by the format. You must NOT judge whether conforming to the format is good, whether the format is well used, or whether the template is a hard or easy one.
proposals.rationale: The disagreement in this slice is heavily stratified by contest family rather than by item: every quoted-dialogue-plus-adverb item is dense-high (R02, R05, R10, R23, R24, R28, R48, R52) and every two-word capitalised coinage from the bad-names prompt is card-high (R04, R12, R18, R27, R44, R47, R58). Template shape therefore predicts strongly while being a fact about which container the row came from. Tagged mixed because contests genuinely differ in how much room they leave for a good entry.
proposals.upstream_parent: container identity - which weekly contest the item was drawn from, and the difficulty and crowding of that contest's entry pool

proposals.name: Verbatim echo of the prompt's own category wording
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH of the text is occupied by language lifted straight from the prompt, the category heading, or the answering apparatus rather than by the submitter's own words. 10 = the text is essentially the prompt's own phrasing restated, or a heading plus a colon, with little or no added material. 5 = the text opens with the prompt's framing formula and then adds its own content. 0 = no prompt language reappears in the entry. Compute this as a rough proportion of the text that is echoed material. You must NOT judge whether echoing is lazy or whether restating the prompt is a legitimate move; report extent only.
proposals.rationale: Several card-high rows are almost pure prompt echo - R33 ('Something That Will Never Become'), R46 ('Something That Will Never Become an Olympic Sport --'), R15 ('A Political Slogan That Will Never Make It:') - and R07 and R34 both begin with the bare apparatus word 'Answer:'. Echo makes an item look maximally on-topic to any topical-fit check while contributing nothing that a submitter wrote, so it is a textbook predictive-but-not-quality surface channel.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Raw length, clause count and syntactic elaboration
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW LONG and syntactically elaborated the text is, in absolute terms. 10 = multiple sentences or many subordinate clauses, roughly 30 words or more, with embedded qualifications. 5 = one full sentence of ordinary length. 0 = a bare phrase of one to three words. Count words and clauses; ignore verse line breaks and count the running text. You must NOT judge whether the length is appropriate to the format, whether the text is padded or economical, or whether brevity is a virtue here. This is a raw size measurement.
proposals.rationale: Among the prose items, the two longest strings in the slice are both card-high - R54 (a three-clause anecdote) and R32 (a heavily front-loaded question about estimating a basketball player's height) - while the shortest strings are dense-high, R41 ('Monosyllabic', one word) and R55 ('I'M WITH STUPID'). Raw size is trivially readable by any model and correlates with per-criterion elaboration credit. Tagged mixed because economy is arguably a real virtue in this format, so the discounted and undiscounted readouts should both be reported.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Title-Case coinage typography versus quoted-dialogue typography
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 on a single typographic axis: how much the text is formatted as a capitalised noun-phrase label rather than as running quoted speech. 10 = the whole entry is a Title Case or ALL CAPS noun phrase with no sentence punctuation and no quotation marks. 5 = mixed, e.g. a sentence containing a capitalised coined label. 0 = the entry is running text inside quotation marks, punctuated as speech, with sentence-case interior. Score only capitalisation pattern, quotation marks and terminal punctuation. You must NOT judge whether the typography is apt for the prompt or whether the label is a clever one.
proposals.rationale: The capitalised-label typography clusters on the card-high side - R12 ('Golden Reliever'), R18 ('Buttdragging Grasshound'), R27 ('USS Powderkeg'), R47 ('Java Screen Freezer'), R58 ('Precision Pi Calculator'), R16 ('The Heimlich Manure'), R01 ('Larry of Arabia') - whereas quoted-speech typography clusters on the dense-high side (R10, R23, R35, R59). Because the typographic split is nearly collinear with the contest-family split, a model can score this surface pattern alone and reproduce much of the disagreement without reading the joke.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Density of period-locked contemporaneous referents
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 for HOW MUCH the text depends on referents that were specific to a narrow window of time - named officeholders, then-current scandals, then-current sports personnel, consumer technology of the moment. 10 = the text cannot be parsed at all without recalling a specific person or event that was in the news within a short period. 5 = one dated referent, but the sentence still parses without it. 0 = wholly timeless content with no period-bound referent. Score the density and load-bearingness of dated references. You must NOT judge whether the topicality is well used, whether the reference is obscure, or whether a modern reader would find it funny; being unable to decode a reference is not a reason to score it lower on this channel - a reference you cannot decode is a MAXIMALLY period-locked one.
proposals.rationale: Period-locked referents saturate the dense-high half (R10 John Bobbitt, R28 Zoe Baird, R02 Mitch Williams, R48 Richie Petitbon, R30 the low-speed televised pursuit, R36 a specific fertility-fraud physician, R42 two accused spies) and are much thinner in the card-high half (R12, R47, R58 are timeless coinages). A judge in a later era will systematically under-read the dated items, so this channel tracks the contest's date and the reader's distance from it rather than the entry's merit. Tagged mixed because sharp topicality was genuinely prized in this format.
proposals.upstream_parent: the date of the containing contest within the multi-year run of the column, and the subsequent decay of its referents

proposals.name: First-available reading of the prompt versus late-stream riff
proposals.instruction: MODE 3, position fingerprint. Score 0-10 for HOW FAR the item reads like a response written after the obvious responses were already in the pile. 10 = the entry visibly steps past the most available reading: it targets an oblique or abstract instance, presupposes that the direct pun has been used, or riffs on the prompt's premise rather than answering it head-on. 5 = a moderately available response, one of perhaps a dozen a reader might generate. 0 = the single most available response to the prompt - the first pun, name, or substitution almost any reader would produce within seconds. Ask yourself only: how far down the list of candidate responses would this one appear? You must NOT judge whether obviousness is bad or whether obliqueness is clever; report position in the availability ordering only. You cannot see the item's real position in the entry stream and must not guess at it - score only the textual fingerprint.
proposals.rationale: The card-high half is dominated by first-available responses: R44 ('WordPrefect') is the single obvious pun on that software name, and R60 ('Peace Corpse'), R16 ('The Heimlich Manure'), R57 ('Profiles in Scourge') and R01 ('Larry of Arabia') are each the first letter-swap anyone would reach for, while R56 reproduces an already-circulating chiasmus. The dense-high half repeatedly steps past the obvious - R41 ('Monosyllabic') and R40 ('Yom Kippur') answer the oxymoron prompt with self-referential and cultural cases rather than the stock 'jumbo shrimp' family, and R19 ('Adam and Eve') picks the one pairing for which the song title becomes a logical fact. Availability ordering is a plausible fingerprint of when in the stream an entry was written, which is upstream of reception for reasons unrelated to the text; it is tagged mixed because working past the obvious is also partly a real skill.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream and submission timing (how early or late relative to other entrants working the same prompt)

proposals.name: Multi-layered simultaneous wordplay
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how many distinct, independent meanings or resonances the entry's central wordplay activates at once. 10 = the pun/phrase works on two or more genuinely separate semantic layers simultaneously (e.g. it is literally true of the referenced person's public reputation AND fits the contest's formal template AND carries a secondary double meaning). 0 = a single flat, one-layer substitution with no secondary resonance beyond the obvious swap.
proposals.rationale: R16 ('anticlimactically' for Pee-wee Herman) and R38 ('disappointedly' for Zoe Baird, punning on dis-appointed/withdrawn-nomination) both stack a generic Tom Swifty adverb-match with a second layer tied to the person's real situation, while R08 ('Golden Reliever') is a flat single-layer swap; this layering gap plausibly explains why dense ranks the former much higher than the scorecard does.

proposals.name: Topical/biographical knowledge required to resolve joke
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry's comedic payoff depends on the reader already knowing a specific real-world scandal, event, or fact tied to a named person or institution, versus being resolvable purely from the words on the page. 10 = the entry is inert or meaningless without that outside knowledge. 0 = fully self-contained; no external knowledge of any specific event is needed.
proposals.rationale: R11 ('Dr. Cecil Jacobson for Jiffy Pop Popcorn') only lands if the reader knows Jacobson's fertility-fraud scandal, and R56 ('Richie Petitbon said absently') only lands if the reader knows Petitbon's disastrous playoff coaching record; both score high dense/low card, unlike self-contained R33 (chiasmus).

proposals.name: Punchline completeness (not a bare fragment)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 whether the entry text contains a full, landed joke (setup and payoff both present) versus a bare category header, title-only fragment, or text that is cut off before any payoff appears. 10 = a complete joke is legible start to finish. 0 = only a header/lead-in/title is present with no discernible punchline in the text.
proposals.rationale: R02 ('A Political Slogan That Will Never Make It:') and R37 ('Something That Will Never Become') give only the category framing with no actual slogan or payoff text, yet both score very high on card_pct; a completeness check would flag these as unscoreable as jokes even though the scorecard rated them highly.

proposals.name: Constructed twist vs. mechanical single-word swap
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the degree to which the humor is a genuinely constructed misdirection or twist rather than one mechanical word/letter substitution dropped into an existing well-known phrase. 10 = built joke with setup and a real twist, not reducible to a single swapped word. 0 = the entire entry is just one existing phrase with one word swapped, no other invention.
proposals.rationale: R53 ('Larry of Arabia') and R41 ('Who wrote "Profiles in Scourge"?') are each a single mechanical name/word swap into a famous title, both dense_low/card_high, contrasted with R42's limerick which builds a full narrative twist (insurance denial) and scores dense_high.

proposals.name: Self-referential meta-humor about form or contest
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry's humor depends on commenting on, or being ironic about, its own construction, the literary form it is written in, or the Style Invitational contest itself. 10 = the joke's core mechanism is this kind of self-awareness. 0 = no self-reference of any kind.
proposals.rationale: R58 ('Monosyllabic' as an entry for 'oxymoron', ironic because the word itself is not monosyllabic) and R13 (an essayistic confession about entering the contest itself, 'I'm almost relieved when I don't win') both rely on this self-aware move and both score dense_high/card_low.

proposals.name: Crude/taboo content as sole comedic engine
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry's laugh depends on scatological, sexual, or taboo subject matter carrying the joke essentially by itself, with little additional wit layered on top. 10 = shock/crude content alone is doing nearly all the work. 0 = no reliance on taboo content; humor (if any) comes from elsewhere.
proposals.rationale: R23 ('The Heimlich Manure') and R36 ('1, 2, breasts . . .') both lean on scatological/sexual content for the whole joke and both are dense_low/card_high, suggesting the scorecard may over-credit crude one-trick puns that the dense model discounts as unsophisticated.

proposals.name: Narrative/scene construction vs. isolated label
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 whether the entry builds an actual mini-scene, situation, or story with internal development, versus stating a single isolated phrase, name, or label with no scene around it. 10 = a full narrative or scene unfolds within the entry. 0 = entry is a single isolated label/phrase, no scene at all.
proposals.rationale: R42 (a full four-line limerick narrative about denied insurance) and R30 (a mini plot summary that logically re-derives 'Peter Pan' from a fugitive-movie premise) both construct scenes and both score dense_high/card_low, unlike single-label entries like R08.

proposals.name: Absurdist juxtaposition of unrelated concrete objects
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how strongly the entry places semantically unrelated, concrete nouns or images side by side for surreal effect, rather than relying on conventional single-domain wordplay. 10 = strong surreal juxtaposition of two or more unrelated concrete items/images. 0 = no juxtaposition; conventional single-domain pun or plain statement.
proposals.rationale: R01 ('A Squeegee and a Codpiece but Not Madeleine Albright') stacks three unrelated concrete items and scores dense_low/card_high despite the strong juxtaposition, and R34 ('Hugging, Kissing and Kvetching') mixes affectionate and Yiddish-register terms; this criterion tests whether juxtaposition alone predicts either model's score.

proposals.name: Register mismatch between solemn frame and mundane/crude target
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how strongly the entry pairs a high-register, solemn, or formal reference frame (religion, tragedy, ceremony, formal institution) with a low, mundane, or crude target, or vice versa. 10 = strong, clear incongruous pairing of a solemn/formal frame with mundane/crude content. 0 = tone is uniform throughout; no such mismatch.
proposals.rationale: R51 ('Bob loved the all-you-can-eat communion') pairs a religious sacrament with a buffet, and R06 ('Yom Kippur' proposed as an oxymoron) frames a solemn holy day ironically; both are dense_high/card_low, unlike tonally flat entries like a plain sports headline.

proposals.name: Genuine trivia/fact masquerading as invented joke
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry is simply a real, verifiable historical or biographical fact/name stated plainly, with no invented comedic twist layered on top, versus a fully invented, non-factual comedic construction. 10 = entry is essentially a straight factual statement or real name/answer with no constructed joke. 0 = entry is entirely invented, non-factual wordplay.
proposals.rationale: R28 and R47 both give the real historical name 'Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim' (Paracelsus) verbatim as a 'Jeopardy' answer with no invented twist, and both score notably high on card_pct (.876, .897) despite modest dense_pct (.321-.324), unlike invented puns such as R20 ('Who founded the Peace Corpse?').

proposals.name: Tom-Swiftly adverb double-resonance with quote and persona
proposals.instruction: For quote-attribution (Tom Swifty) style entries, score 0-10 how precisely the chosen adverb's literal meaning connects, punningly, to BOTH the literal content of the quoted words AND the real-world identity/situation of the named speaker, versus merely describing a generic manner of speaking. 10 = the adverb resonates precisely with both the quote's wording and the speaker's real context. 0 = adverb only loosely sets a tone, no wordplay connection to either.
proposals.rationale: R27 ('circumspectly' for John Bobbitt, punning on 'circum-' and his real-world case) and R24 ('cordially' for Ted Kennedy, punning on 'cordial' as a liqueur alongside his public drinking reputation) both achieve this double resonance and score dense_high/card_low, unlike single-layer instances like R16 ('anticlimactically').

proposals.name: Formal-structure discipline (meter/rhyme/reversal precision)
proposals.instruction: For entries constrained by a named literary form (limerick, chiasmus, Tom Swifty, haiku, etc.), score 0-10 how precisely and cleanly the entry satisfies that form's meter, rhyme scheme, grammatical reversal, or other structural constraint. 10 = the form is executed with no metrical, rhyme, or structural flaws. 0 = the form is badly broken, ignored, or barely attempted.
proposals.rationale: R19 (the chiasmus 'Being nice isn't easy, and being easy isn't nice' executes a clean AB/BA reversal) and R42 (the limerick keeps clean AABBA rhyme and meter across all five lines) both score dense_low/card_high, testing whether mechanical form-compliance alone is driving the scorecard's high ratings independent of actual wit.

proposals.name: Economy: comedic payoff per word
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the ratio of comedic payoff to text length: how much of the joke's full effect is delivered in very few words versus requiring a long wind-up to reach a comparably small payoff. 10 = maximal payoff landed in a handful of words. 0 = long entry required to arrive at a comparably small or absent payoff.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('I'M WITH STUPID', three words, full payoff) and R60 ('U.N. Resolution', two words) both land completely in minimal text and score dense_high/card_low, contrasted with the much longer paragraph-length R13 which delivers a comparatively soft single joke.

proposals.name: Formatting-artifact contamination (non-substantive fragments)
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of the entry's visible text is non-substantive formatting residue (a bare cartoon-caption dash, a repeated/redundant 'Answer:' prefix, a sentence cut off mid-word) rather than assessable comedic content. 10 = the item is essentially formatting noise with no assessable comedic content (e.g., just '--' or a duplicated header). 0 = the entry is fully substantive comedic text with no formatting contamination.
proposals.rationale: R48 ('(Cartoon D) --') and R52 ('(Cartoon E) --') contain almost no assessable content beyond a cartoon label and a dash, yet both post extremely high dense_pct (.997, .998); R15 ('(Cartoon A) This is a beguiling') is similarly cut off mid-sentence, raising the possibility that near-empty text is spuriously inflating dense scores for this prompt type.

proposals.name: Dependence on the contest prompt to become legible
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry only becomes interpretable or funny when read alongside its specific contest prompt, versus standing on its own as a joke even if shown with no prompt at all. 10 = entry is fully opaque or meaningless without the specific prompt's framing. 0 = entry would land as a joke even presented with zero context about the prompt.
proposals.rationale: R05 ('The Secret Agent's Lament', just a title) only registers as ironic once paired with the 'bad Valentine's poetry' prompt, and R33 ('Adam and Eve: "It Had to Be You"') only works once paired with the 'wrong wedding song' prompt structure; both are dense_high/card_low, unlike prompt-independent entries like R23 ('The Heimlich Manure').

proposals.name: Presence of parenthetical author-attribution tag
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much of a complete parenthetical attribution tag -- e.g. '(Name, City)' or multiple such name/city pairs -- appears attached to the entry text. 0 = no attribution tag present at all; 10 = a fully formed one (or more) name-and-city attribution appears. This is an extent measure of a formatting/template feature only; do not judge whether the entry or its attribution is good.
proposals.rationale: R48 ('Bob loved the all-you-can-eat communion. (Chuck Smith, Woodbridge)') and R54 ('Lesser Hyattsville (David Genser, Arlington)') carry full attribution tags while R11 ('The Secret Agent's Lament') and R57 ('Something That Will Never Become') carry none; attribution presence is a transcription/template habit, not a property of how funny the entry is, yet it may correlate with which rows either model favors purely because of formatting.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: All-caps / heavy-capitalization typography
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the extent of non-standard heavy capitalization in the entry text (e.g., whole words or the whole entry rendered in ALL CAPS beyond normal sentence/title case). 0 = standard case throughout; 10 = entry is predominantly ALL CAPS. Score only the amount of capitalization present; do not judge whether the capitalization makes the entry better or worse.
proposals.rationale: R32 ('I'M WITH STUPID') is fully capitalized in a T-shirt-design prompt and scores dense_high/card_low; capitalization here may be tracking the shirt-slogan genre/medium convention rather than joke quality, though punchier all-caps delivery could also genuinely read as funnier, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: the physical medium/genre convention implied by the contest prompt (e.g., a T-shirt-slogan prompt conventionally invites all-caps text, independent of the entrant's actual wit)

proposals.name: Trailing dash/ellipsis truncation mark
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry's visible text ends abruptly in a truncating mark (a dash '--', an ellipsis '...', or similar) immediately after the last word, as opposed to ending with ordinary terminal punctuation or none. 0 = entry ends normally; 10 = entry text ends with a dash/ellipsis suggestive of a cut-off transcription. Score only the presence of this punctuation pattern; do not judge whether the entry is funnier or worse for ending this way.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('Something That Will Never Become an Olympic Sport --') and R56 ('(Cartoon D) --') both end in a bare trailing dash with no further words, which looks like a data-capture/formatting artifact rather than a deliberate comedic choice, yet both carry unusually extreme percentile scores from one of the two models.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only (a transcription or corpus-extraction artifact upstream of the entry's actual content)

proposals.name: Named real-world public-figure/institution density
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how many distinct real-world public figures or institutions are referred to by name in the entry text (count/density only). 0 = no named real-world person or institution appears; 10 = multiple distinct named real-world figures/institutions appear. Score only how many are named; do not judge whether the reference is used cleverly or is funny.
proposals.rationale: R03 (John Bobbitt) and R29 (Dr. Cecil Jacobson) both name a specific real public figure because their prompts structurally require it; since named-figure density is largely forced by prompt genre rather than chosen for wit, either model could be spuriously tracking prompt-genre membership through this feature -- though skilled writers may also better exploit named figures for real wit, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: the contest prompt's own explicit formal requirement in several prompts to include 'a reference to a famous person or institution' (a structural, prompt-driven feature rather than a discretionary authorial quality choice)

proposals.name: Tom-Swiftly canonical template conformity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how precisely the entry follows the canonical Tom-Swifty template ('[quoted words],' [Name] [said/verb] [manner-adverb]. (Attributor, City)), purely as a structural/template match. 0 = entry does not follow this template at all; 10 = entry matches the template's quote+attribution-verb+adverb+credit structure exactly. Score only template conformity; do not judge whether the specific pun within it is clever.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R59 both reproduce the exact quote-verb-adverb-attribution template with no structural deviation; fluent template reproduction may be tracking authorial practice/seniority in the format rather than the cleverness of this particular pun, though practiced authors may also genuinely write better puns, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice/familiarity with this specific literary sub-genre (a seasoned contest entrant who has written many Tom Swiftlys before and reproduces the template fluently)

proposals.name: Grammatical/prose polish independent of joke content
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 the grammatical complexity, punctuation correctness, and sentence-level polish of the entry's prose, independent of whether its underlying idea is funny. 0 = rough, fragmentary, or ungrammatical text; 10 = fully polished, grammatically complete, correctly punctuated prose. Score only surface polish; do not judge whether the entry is funny.
proposals.rationale: R36's limerick is fully polished, grammatically complete verse across four lines, while R57 ('Something That Will Never Become') is a bare sentence fragment; polish level may track authorial practice/editing rather than the wit of the underlying idea, though more practiced writers may also write funnier entries, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's general writing practice/education, or possible upstream editorial smoothing before the entry reached this corpus

proposals.name: Joint/multiple-entrant crediting on one entry
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how many distinct named entrants (name+city pairs) are credited together on this single entry. 0 = a single credited entrant or none; 10 = three or more distinct entrants credited jointly on the same entry. Score only the count of co-credited entrants; do not judge whether joint crediting makes the entry better.
proposals.rationale: R31 ('Sandra Hull, Arlington, and Stu Solomon, Springfield') and R52 ('Paul Styrene, Olney; Elden Carnahan, Laurel') are each credited to two independent entrants on one entry, a textual trace of idea-convergence/crowding in the submission pool rather than of this particular execution's wit.
proposals.upstream_parent: crowding of the entry-pool container (multiple independent entrants submitted the same or a near-identical idea, so the editor credited more than one of them together -- a fingerprint of how common/obvious that specific idea was among the whole submission stream)

proposals.name: Direct restatement of prompt's own vocabulary
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry's central wording directly reuses or closely paraphrases the specific key terms given in its own contest prompt, versus introducing vocabulary/concepts several inferential steps removed from the prompt's literal wording. 0 = entry shares essentially no vocabulary or concepts with the prompt's literal wording; 10 = entry's core content is built almost verbatim from the prompt's own key terms. Score only the degree of verbal overlap/directness; do not judge whether this makes the entry funnier.
proposals.rationale: R07 ('Something That Will Never Become an Olympic Sport --') and R57 ('Something That Will Never Become') both restate their 'things that will never happen' prompt's own clause almost verbatim with minimal inferential distance, unlike a more removed entry such as R08 ('Precision Pi Calculator'); directness of restatement may be a fingerprint of an early, obvious submission rather than of joke quality, though the most obvious reading can occasionally also be the tightest/funniest one, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: the item's position early in the submission stream (an obvious, first-pass reading of the prompt that a writer produces before seeing more inventive later takes accumulate in the pool)

proposals.name: Narrow/recent real-world news-cycle specificity
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how narrow and temporally specific the entry's real-world reference appears to be, based only on how it is worded (e.g., naming a very particular, then-current scandal/event with recency-coded phrasing) versus a broad, evergreen, or undated reference. 0 = no time-specific real-world reference, or a purely evergreen one; 10 = a highly specific reference that reads as tied to a narrow, recent news window. Score only the apparent narrowness/recency of the reference as written; do not judge whether the topical reference is funny.
proposals.rationale: R14 ('My name has been withdrawn,' said Zoe Baird disappointedly) reads as tied to a narrow nomination-withdrawal news window, and R29 (Dr. Cecil Jacobson for Jiffy Pop) references a specific scandal, unlike evergreen entries such as R33's chiasmus with no topical reference at all; recency/specificity of the reference may track submission timing relative to a news cycle rather than the entry's constructed wit, though very fresh references can also genuinely land better with contemporaneous judges, hence mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: timing of the item's production relative to a fresh news cycle (the author writing very soon after a breaking real-world event, versus drawing on an older or evergreen reference)

proposals.name: Interrogative/question-form surface syntax
proposals.instruction: Score 0-10 how much the entry's surface syntax takes question form (begins with an interrogative word such as 'What,' 'Who,' 'Why,' or 'How,' and/or ends with a question mark). 0 = entry is not phrased as a question at all; 10 = entry is fully phrased as a direct question in both opening word and terminal punctuation. Score only this surface syntactic feature; do not judge whether the question itself is clever.
proposals.rationale: R21 ('What is the opposite of a head count?') and R37 ('Who wrote "Profiles in Scourge"?') both take full interrogative surface form as required by their Jeopardy-style prompt, unlike declarative entries such as R18 ('USS Powderkeg'); this syntactic marker is largely a prompt-genre template effect rather than a signal of the entry's own comedic quality.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only (a template feature largely forced by the 'Jeopardy!' prompt's own answer-to-question genre requirement, not an independent authorial quality choice)

proposals.name: Executable Prompt Fulfillment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry fully performs the requested task with a finished comic act; score 0 when it is only a heading, label, fragment, or restatement of the prompt.
proposals.rationale: R04, R06, R09, and R44 stop before supplying a usable joke, while R23 and R37 actually execute their requested forms.

proposals.name: Mutual Semantic Lock
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry’s parts make one another newly meaningful or surprising; score 0 when its parts merely coexist without a reciprocal connection.
proposals.rationale: The quoted statements and adverbs in R14, R20, and R31 create linked meanings, unlike the loosely assembled components in R28.

proposals.name: Conversational Naturalness
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording sounds effortless and believable aloud while retaining the comic twist; score 0 when it sounds syntactically assembled, forced, or unlike plausible speech.
proposals.rationale: R14, R18, and R20 use smoothly speakable dialogue around unusual adverbs, whereas many formally correct constructions can feel mechanically generated.

proposals.name: Reference With Comic Function
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a cultural or personal reference actively creates the joke’s tension or reversal; score 0 when the reference is merely decorative or obscure without comic work.
proposals.rationale: The figures in R16, R33, and R55 supply the central contrast, while the long proper name in R08 can stand without generating an additional idea.

proposals.name: Self-Contained Payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry provides enough context for a reader to understand both setup and payoff from the text alone; score 0 when it depends on missing context or supplies no payoff.
proposals.rationale: R01 and R23 contain their own situations and resolutions, while R08, R13, and R50 are largely bare names or labels.

proposals.name: Escalating List Architecture
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when successive list items intensify, redirect, or sharpen the joke and the final item lands strongest; score 0 when the items are interchangeable or randomly accumulated.
proposals.rationale: R23 escalates through increasingly absurd objects before its final image, while R28 presents a list whose elements have little cumulative development.

proposals.name: Cliché Reassignment
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a familiar slogan, quotation, or title is relocated so its usual implication becomes newly comic; score 0 when the familiar phrase remains unchanged or is attached arbitrarily.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R29 repurpose recognizable slogans through their contest context, while R40 relies more directly on a familiar song title without a comparable reassignment.

proposals.name: Readable Contradiction
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an apparent contradiction follows from a precise, instantly understandable clash of meanings; score 0 when it is merely short, technically paradoxical, or semantically arbitrary.
proposals.rationale: R17’s “Low-Speed Chase” presents a clean semantic collision, while R54’s “Yom Kippur” offers much less evident contradiction from the text alone.

proposals.name: Logical Collapse Depth
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a statement initially sounds sensible but fails under a specific second reading; score 0 when it is a truism, tautology, or merely grammatical statement.
proposals.rationale: R12 and R38 invite assent before undermining their own logic, whereas R37 mainly reverses familiar words without a comparable collapse.

proposals.name: Specificity That Pictures a Scene
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when concrete details sharply evoke a visual, social, or physical situation that drives the humor; score 0 when the wording remains generic and image-free.
proposals.rationale: Tysons Corner and rejected insurance in R01, the bank queue in R36, and the named product pairing in R55 create vivid situations rather than abstract wordplay alone.

proposals.name: Sonic Payoff
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when rhyme, rhythm, alliteration, or sound resemblance makes the punchline feel both surprising and inevitable; score 0 when sound pattern is absent, forced, or merely decorative.
proposals.rationale: R01 uses “forlorner” and “mourn her” for a comic rhyme, and R23 sustains a deliberately crude rhyme scheme whose sounds support the final image.

proposals.name: Pun Precision
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a pun preserves a recognizable source phrase while producing a coherent second meaning; score 0 when it is only a typo, loose homophone, or phonetic resemblance without a meaningful shift.
proposals.rationale: R27, R39, and R59 each make recognizable phrases do new semantic work, while similar-looking constructions can stop at surface word substitution.

proposals.name: Form as Comic Engine
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the required genre or structure generates an additional layer of humor; score 0 when the form merely wraps a generic line without affecting its meaning.
proposals.rationale: The reversal in R37 depends on chiasmus, and the definition format in R42 supports its joke, whereas the headline in R22 reads like an ordinary statement.

proposals.name: Perspective Reversal
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry makes a familiar institution, relationship, or activity absurd by shifting the reader’s viewpoint; score 0 when it merely describes an odd object or situation.
proposals.rationale: R34 reframes communion through buffet language, R35 reframes presidential propriety, and R55 turns endorsement itself into the comic target.

proposals.name: Purposeful Minimalism
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when very few words trigger a clear, satisfying inference that completes the joke; score 0 when brevity leaves only an unfinished or opaque fragment.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R29 are compact but invite specific contextual interpretations, while R04 and R06 are short because the requested comic act never occurs.

proposals.name: Morphological wordplay
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 (absent) to 10 (pervasive) how much the entry uses spelling changes, homophones, portmanteaus, or near-word substitutions. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the wordplay is good, funny, or effective.
proposals.rationale: A text system may latch onto conspicuous lexical mutations as an easy humor proxy, although their presence does not establish entry quality. Examples include R27, R36, and R45.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Prompt-template scaffolding
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the entry contains prompt labels, category headings, answer shells, quotation numbering, trailing colons, or dashes. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the format is good or appropriate.
proposals.rationale: Experienced participants may leave recognizable contest-format residue, which can correlate with both familiarity and genuine craft; the residue itself is not quality. Examples include R13, R17, R29, and R52.
proposals.upstream_parent: author's practice in the format

proposals.name: Byline metadata residue
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the visible text includes appended author names, locations, or single-author parenthetical credits rather than entry content. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the credited author or entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Names and locations can act as proxies for reputation, familiarity, or local identity, while practiced authors may also write better entries. Examples include R04, R07, and R51.
proposals.upstream_parent: author reputation, following, or geography

proposals.name: Joint-authorship trace
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the entry visibly presents two or more credited contributors or an explicit collaborative authorship trace. Judge only extent; do not judge whether collaboration improved the entry.
proposals.rationale: Collaboration can leave an observable plural-credit fingerprint and can also genuinely improve writing, making this a mixed nuisance. Examples include R24, R35, and R36.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing or assistance

proposals.name: Unfilled-slot residue
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the entry reads as a bare prompt-shaped placeholder: a category restatement, title fragment, trailing colon or dash, or missing-looking payload. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the response is good or complete.
proposals.rationale: An early literal take, late rushed submission, or crowded-container residue may produce this textual trace; the trace is a nuisance signal rather than evidence of merit. Examples include R02, R17, and R52.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream or submission timing

proposals.name: Transmission artifacts
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the text contains visible encoding or transcription irregularities such as replacement glyphs, doubled quotation marks, malformed punctuation, or corrupted characters. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the resulting text is good or readable.
proposals.rationale: Formatting pipelines can create artifacts that a text model treats as distinctive style, even though they say nothing about the entry itself. Examples include R05, R06, and R28.
proposals.upstream_parent: publication, transcription, or ingestion pipeline

proposals.name: Dated cultural anchoring
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the entry depends on period-bound people, technologies, institutions, or media, such as obsolete devices or strongly era-specific references. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the references are good or funny.
proposals.rationale: Temporal familiarity and nostalgia can affect how text is processed independently of its construction as an entry. Examples include R05, R51, and R60.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience cohort and temporal distance

proposals.name: Taboo-register load
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the entry uses explicit sexual, anatomical, excretory, or sacrilegious vocabulary or imagery. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the taboo material is good, funny, or acceptable.
proposals.rationale: Taboo vocabulary can trigger audience and moderation reactions that are separate from intrinsic entry quality. Examples include R19, R25, R44, and R54.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience taste and social acceptability

proposals.name: Named-entity dependence
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much understanding the entry visibly depends on named people, places, brands, institutions, programs, or titles. Judge only the amount of shared-world reference; do not judge whether the references are good or apt.
proposals.rationale: Recognition of names can create a reception shortcut for a text-only system without measuring the entry's construction. Examples include R05, R07, R24, and R51.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience familiarity with cultural references

proposals.name: Venue-insider language
proposals.instruction: Rate from 0 to 10 how much the entry directly invokes the Style Invitational, Washington Post, contest culture, recurring slogans, or recognizable venue symbols. Judge only extent; do not judge whether the insider reference is good or effective.
proposals.rationale: Venue familiarity may leave self-referential language and may also help an author understand the format genuinely well, so the channel is a sensitivity band. Examples include R10, R39, R42, and R59.
proposals.upstream_parent: venue and community familiarity

proposals.name: Delayed Reinterpretation
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when an initially straightforward reading is cleanly overturned by a later phrase into a second coherent joke; score 0 when the entry has only one obvious reading or no meaningful turn.
proposals.rationale: R03 and R32 both invite an initial literal reading before their names or plot descriptions acquire a more pointed comic meaning.

proposals.name: Exact Compression
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when nearly every word performs setup, contrast, or punchline work with no removable padding; score 0 when the entry is verbose, generic, or contains expendable wording.
proposals.rationale: R04, R13, R51, and R60 demonstrate how extremely short phrases can carry a complete, highly targeted comic mechanism.

proposals.name: Form-Driven Humor
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the contest's required form itself generates the humor, rather than merely containing it; score 0 when the entry could be pasted into another format unchanged.
proposals.rationale: The adverbial structure in R17 and R22, and the literal plot-summary constraint in R32, are integral to their jokes rather than decorative packaging.

proposals.name: Adverbial Lock
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the final adverb is grammatically natural, describes the speaker's delivery, and sharply changes or contradicts the statement; score 0 when the adverb is generic or merely grammatical.
proposals.rationale: R17, R22, R41, and R44 show how a precisely chosen adverb can simultaneously complete the sentence and supply its comic reversal.

proposals.name: Reference Necessity
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the named person or institution is indispensable to the joke and contributes specific semantic tension; score 0 when the reference is interchangeable celebrity decoration.
proposals.rationale: The identities in R17, R22, and R55 determine why the quoted statements are funny; replacing them would substantially weaken the mechanism.

proposals.name: Deadpan Subject Mismatch
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when grave, taboo, or embarrassing subject matter is expressed in an unnervingly calm and fittingly mundane tone; score 0 when tone and subject naturally match or create no tension.
proposals.rationale: R15, R55, and R58 pair reputationally charged subjects with matter-of-fact language, creating humor through controlled tonal dissonance.

proposals.name: Contest-Aware Metahumor
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry comments on contests, media, or the act of submitting humor while remaining a functioning joke; score 0 when it is a generic statement unrelated to that machinery.
proposals.rationale: R13, R21, and R51 derive extra force from recognizable contest or slogan conventions rather than operating as context-free jokes.

proposals.name: Defensible Literal Twist
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a literal interpretation of a premise produces an unexpected but textually defensible comic consequence; score 0 when the twist is random, factually unsupported, or merely repeats the premise.
proposals.rationale: R20 turns an insurance detail into a literal tragic consequence, while R32 extracts an exact but surprising description from a familiar story.

proposals.name: Yogi-ism Logical Collapse
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a sentence initially resembles sensible wisdom but collapses under a precise internal contradiction or category error; score 0 when it is an ordinary truism or undisciplined nonsense.
proposals.rationale: R11 and R50 both sound aphoristic at first, then fail because their own wording makes the supposed insight circular or self-defeating.

proposals.name: Reality-Anchored Oxymoron
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when contradictory terms collide around a recognizable real-world institution, practice, or situation; score 0 when the phrase is merely two unrelated opposites.
proposals.rationale: R04, R34, R39, and R60 make their contradictions feel specific by attaching them to familiar political, religious, linguistic, or public-safety realities.

proposals.name: Phonetic Pun Payload
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when a recognizable phrase is transformed by sound into a new expression whose altered meaning is itself relevant; score 0 when the near-homophone is arbitrary or has no semantic payload.
proposals.rationale: R38, R53, and R56 show the difference between a merely similar-sounding replacement and one that creates a concrete second meaning.

proposals.name: Reversible Jeopardy Fit
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry functions unmistakably as an answer with a clear, uniquely motivated question implied by its wording; score 0 when it is just a name, fragment, or question-answer mismatch.
proposals.rationale: R05, R08, R10, R24, and R48 illustrate how recognizable material can still lack a well-formed, recoverable Jeopardy relationship.

proposals.name: Standalone Completion
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the entry is a complete joke or answer without requiring a missing category, image, label, or continuation; score 0 when it reads like a heading, placeholder, or unfinished submission.
proposals.rationale: R06, R31, R35, and R46 are structurally incomplete on their face, so formal compliance alone should not substitute for a finished comic payoff.

proposals.name: Vivid Comic Scene
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when the wording creates a specific, easily pictured situation that carries the humor; score 0 when it remains an abstract label or unelaborated assertion.
proposals.rationale: R09 supplies the striking image of all-you-can-eat communion, while R20 supplies concrete medical, insurance, and social details that make its premise vivid.

proposals.name: Rhyme as Semantic Engine
proposals.instruction: Score 10 when rhyme, meter, and line endings advance the premise, escalate the imagery, and deliver the final turn; score 0 when rhyme merely fills a formal requirement.
proposals.rationale: R14 uses a sequence of increasingly outrageous mooning targets before its final image, and R20 makes its rhymes carry the narrative from illness to rejection to consequence.

proposals.name: Byline metadata
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much explicit author, location, or contributor-credit metadata is shown; judge only its presence, never whether the entry is good.
proposals.rationale: Visible credits occur in R01 and R04, while other entries omit them. Such metadata can proxy an author's status or familiarity with the format without describing the entry's substantive properties.
proposals.upstream_parent: author reputation, following, or established entrant status

proposals.name: Coauthor signature
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the text visibly signals multiple authors, joint credit, or collaborative production; do not judge whether collaboration improves the entry.
proposals.rationale: R24 credits two contributors and R49 credits Michelle and Warren Uhler. Collaboration can alter how a submission is treated and can also affect the actual construction of the text, so this channel is mixed.
proposals.upstream_parent: editing, assistance, or team production

proposals.name: Local-place anchoring
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the substantive entry names recognizable local or regional places; judge only geographic specificity, not whether the reference is funny or effective.
proposals.rationale: R12 names Detroit, R22 names Hyattsville, and R44 names Tysons Corner. Local recognizability can influence reception through community familiarity even though geographic naming alone is not a property of contest fit.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience familiarity, community ties, or local recognition

proposals.name: Contest in-group references
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the entry explicitly mentions the Style Invitational, its newspaper setting, or insider contest culture; do not judge whether that context makes the entry good.
proposals.rationale: R27 mentions The Style Invitational and R28 discusses entering it. Such references can trigger venue-specific familiarity, while deliberate awareness of the contest can also genuinely shape the entry's fit.
proposals.upstream_parent: audience or venue familiarity

proposals.name: Editorial scaffold leakage
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much copied prompt or editorial scaffolding appears, such as answer labels, quote numbers, cartoon labels, or headings; judge only visible scaffolding, never its quality.
proposals.rationale: R03 uses “Cartoon E,” R13 uses “Quote 1,” and R32 begins with “Answer.” These tokens may reflect submission or packaging conventions rather than the substantive text.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission template or editorial packaging

proposals.name: Textual bulk
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for the visible amount of wording and verbosity, from a minimal fragment to a lengthy passage; do not judge whether brevity or length is desirable.
proposals.rationale: R03 is a two-token placeholder-like fragment, whereas R55 is a multi-line verse. Word count and verbosity are easy textual signals that can influence model behavior independently of contest-specific merit.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Typographic ornament
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the entry uses conspicuous capitalization, quotation marks, repeated punctuation, colons, dashes, ellipses, or unusual layout; judge formatting extent only, never whether it helps the joke.
proposals.rationale: R25 is entirely capitalized, while R59 uses quotation marks, a colon, and an ellipsis sequence. Such typography can act as a stable formatting cue unrelated to the entry's underlying construction.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Proper-name density
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how densely the entry contains named people, places, institutions, brands, songs, or titles; count visible entities only and do not judge their appropriateness.
proposals.rationale: R10 contains Richie Petitbon and playoff games, while R37 combines Dr. Cecil Jacobson with Jiffy Pop; R49 adds two names and a song title. Entity density is a topical and lexical signal, not itself a quality attribute.
proposals.upstream_parent: surface-only

proposals.name: Dated cultural markers
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the entry signals a particular past era through people, technology, media, or cultural references; judge temporal explicitness only, never whether the references work.
proposals.rationale: R51 refers to VCRs, R53 to Pee-wee Herman, and R55 to the QE II. Era markers can proxy when or for whom the text was produced, while period alignment can also genuinely affect the entry's contextual fit.
proposals.upstream_parent: submission timing or period-specific cultural familiarity

proposals.name: Prompt-echo minimalism
proposals.instruction: Score 0–10 for how much the substantive entry repeats the prompt's category wording with only a generic or blank completion; judge textual repetition and minimal transformation, never whether that pattern is good.
proposals.rationale: R17 repeats “Something That Will Never” with a category ending, R33 repeats “A Political Slogan That Will Never Make It,” and R38 gives only “Something That Will Never Become.” This can fingerprint an early, first-pass reading or stream position without being a textual quality property.
proposals.upstream_parent: position in the entry stream or submission timing
